requirements: Reproduce the core contributions of 'Deep Kernel Fusion for Transformers' — the DeepFusionKernel operator, its profiler-driven scheduler, its integration with SGLang, and the reported throughput speedups on A100 and H100 GPU clusters for LLaMA 3.1 70B inference workloads.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware, GPU cluster configuration, software stack, framework versions, and interconnect settings required to reproduce all experiments are available and correctly configured.
GPU hardware requirements: an NVIDIA A100 80GB SXM cluster and/or NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM cluster with at least 4 GPUs per node are available for tensor-parallel inference.
A single-node cluster with 4 NVIDIA A100 80GB SXM GPUs is available and accessible for benchmarking, with each GPU's memory verified to be 80 GB.
A single-node cluster with 4 NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM GPUs is available and accessible for benchmarking, with each GPU's memory verified to be 80 GB.

Code has been implemented to detect and report the GPU compute capability (sm_80 for A100, sm_90 for H100) and peak FP16 Tensor Core throughput (312 TFLOPs/s for A100, 1979 TFLOPs/s for H100) prior to running benchmarks.
GPU interconnect topology is configured to expose NVLink between GPU pairs and PCIe for other connections, matching the A100 SXM setup described in Section A.2.
The 4-GPU node is configured such that each pair of GPUs is connected via NVLink (600 GB/s on A100 SXM), verifiable via `nvidia-smi topo -m` or equivalent.
PCIe Gen4 links (64 GB/s) between GPUs and host are present and verifiable, and NCCL is configured to use NVLink where available for all-reduce collectives across TP=4.

The same inter-device reduction strategy (SGLang's custom cross-device all-reduce kernels) is used across all baseline and DeepFusionKernel measurements to isolate fusion effects from communication effects.
The CUDA/driver software stack required for A100 and H100 tensor-core FP16 execution is installed at compatible versions.
A CUDA toolkit version compatible with SGLang v0.4.6.post4, vLLM v0.10.1.1, and PyTorch 2.6.0 (CUDA 12.x) is installed and detected by all frameworks.
The NVIDIA driver installed is recent enough to support both A100 (sm_80) and H100 (sm_90) with CUDA 12.x, and NCCL is installed for multi-GPU collectives.
CUDA Graphs support is enabled and functional in the environment such that SGLang can capture a full CUDA Graph during warm-up without runtime errors.
The Python/PyTorch environment is set up at the exact versions used by the paper, isolated from other installations.
PyTorch version 2.6.0 is installed with CUDA support and can execute a basic FP16 matmul on both A100 and H100 GPUs.
A dedicated Python virtual environment (or container) pins PyTorch 2.6.0, SGLang v0.4.6.post4, and vLLM v0.10.1.1 without version conflicts among their shared dependencies.
Triton (compatible with the CUDA toolkit and PyTorch 2.6.0) is installed so that custom fused kernels used by DeepFusionKernel can be compiled and executed.
The FlashInfer attention backend and related inference accelerators are installed at versions compatible with SGLang v0.4.6.post4.
FlashInfer is installed and can be selected as the attention backend inside SGLang v0.4.6.post4 without runtime errors on both A100 and H100.
SGLang is launched with the FlashInfer backend and CUDA Graphs enabled for all DeepFusionKernel and SGLang baseline measurements, verified via SGLang startup logs.
Tensor-parallel launch configuration and environment variables required for reproducible TP=4 decoding are set correctly.
All experiments are launched with tensor-parallel size TP=4 (SGLang `--tp 4`, vLLM `--tensor-parallel-size 4`, and PyTorch distributed with world size 4) and this is verified in launch logs.
GPU clocks, ECC settings, and MIG mode are configured identically across all four GPUs (MIG disabled, persistence mode on) to reduce measurement variance.
Environment variables CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, NCCL_DEBUG, and NCCL_P2P_LEVEL are set consistently so that all baselines and DeepFusionKernel see the same 4 GPUs and the same NCCL P2P configuration.

LLaMA 3.1 70B (FP16) is obtained under the correct license, and SGLang v0.4.6.post4, vLLM v0.10.1.1, PyTorch 2.6.0, and the FlashInfer attention backend are installed and usable as baseline inference frameworks.
The LLaMA 3.1 70B model is acquired in FP16 precision under its Community License and loadable by the inference frameworks.

Code has been implemented to download or reference LLaMA 3.1 70B weights from the official Hugging Face repository (meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B) using authenticated access consistent with the Llama 3.1 Community License Agreement.
The model weights are stored/loaded in FP16 precision (dtype=float16) as required by the throughput experiments.

The acquired checkpoint reproduces the expected LLaMA 3.1 70B architecture parameters (80 layers, hidden size 8192, d_ff = 28672, SwiGLU MLP) so that the SwiGLU shape assumptions used by DeepFusionKernel hold.
The correct pinned versions of PyTorch, SGLang, and vLLM (with matching licenses) are installed as an operational baseline stack.
PyTorch is installed at version 2.6.0 with CUDA support enabled (torch.cuda.is_available() returns True) matching the paper's reference build.
SGLang is installed at the pinned tag v0.4.6.post4 (Apache-2.0 license) and importable as `sglang`, with its distributed server launchable for LLaMA 3.1 70B.
vLLM is installed at the pinned tag v0.10.1.1 (Apache-2.0 license) and can serve LLaMA 3.1 70B under TP=4 as a baseline framework.
The installed SGLang and vLLM versions expose Python APIs / CLIs (e.g. `python -m sglang.launch_server`, `vllm serve`) that accept the LLaMA 3.1 70B model path and TP-size argument without error.
The FlashInfer attention backend is installed and selectable inside SGLang, with CUDA Graph capture enabled during warm-up.
The FlashInfer package is installed at a version compatible with SGLang v0.4.6.post4 and importable as `flashinfer` without runtime errors on the target GPU (A100 or H100).
SGLang is configured (e.g. `--attention-backend flashinfer`) so that FlashInfer is the active attention backend during all end-to-end throughput measurements.
CUDA Graphs capture is enabled in SGLang during the warm-up phase (default behavior not disabled), so that per-iteration PyTorch/kernel launch overheads are eliminated during measurement.
A smoke test verifies that the acquired model and each framework can run end-to-end inference on LLaMA 3.1 70B before any DeepFusionKernel integration is measured.

A minimal end-to-end sanity script loads LLaMA 3.1 70B in FP16 with TP=4 under both SGLang (FlashInfer backend) and vLLM and successfully generates at least one output token for a prompt of length 1, confirming the baseline stack is usable.

A PyTorch naive distributed inference path for LLaMA 3.1 70B in FP16 with TP=4 is executable end-to-end and produces the same token predictions (greedy decoding) as SGLang for a short reference prompt, confirming the model weights are correctly loaded across frameworks.

The tensor-parallel partitioning scheme for the SwiGLU MLP (W_Up and W_Gate column-wise, W_Down row-wise, single all-reduce per block) is implemented consistently with the paper's Figure 2 and Section A.1.
Column-wise sharding of W_Up and W_Gate is implemented so that each of the TP=4 ranks holds a contiguous slice of the d_ff dimension.
Code has been implemented that constructs sharded W_Up and W_Gate tensors on each rank whose local d_ff dimension equals d_ff / TP (i.e., column-parallel partitioning of the (d_model, d_ff) weight).

Code has been implemented that loads/initializes LLaMA 3.1 70B W_Up and W_Gate weights and distributes them column-wise across the 4 TP ranks with no cross-rank overlap and full coverage of the full weight matrices.
Code has been implemented so that the column-parallel W_Up and W_Gate GEMMs take the full replicated input activation X (of shape (M, d_model)) as input on each rank, without an input all-gather.
Row-wise sharding of W_Down is implemented so that each rank consumes only its local slice of the intermediate activation.
Code has been implemented that shards W_Down row-wise so that each rank holds a (d_ff / TP, d_model) slice, matching the column-parallel output layout of the (SiLU(W_Gate X) * (W_Up X)) intermediate.

Code has been implemented so that the local W_Down GEMM on each rank produces a partial (M, d_model) output tensor from its local intermediate activation shard, with no intermediate all-gather on the d_ff dimension.
The SiLU nonlinearity and elementwise gate multiplication are executed entirely on each rank's local shard without cross-device communication.

Code has been implemented such that SiLU(W_Gate X) and its elementwise multiplication with (W_Up X) operate on the local (M, d_ff / TP) shard on each rank, with no collective operations invoked between the first GEMMs and W_Down.
Exactly one all-reduce collective is issued per SwiGLU MLP block, aggregating the partial W_Down outputs across TP ranks.
Code has been implemented that performs a single all-reduce (sum) on the (M, d_model) partial output tensor after the W_Down GEMM, producing the final replicated SwiGLU block output on every rank.
A behavioral test verifies that exactly one collective communication call (one all-reduce, and zero all-gathers or reduce-scatters) is invoked per SwiGLU MLP block during a decoding step under TP=4.
The implementation reuses SGLang's existing all-reduce / collective primitives for the SwiGLU block's post-W_Down aggregation rather than introducing a new communication routine.
The distributed SwiGLU MLP produces numerically correct outputs matching a single-device reference implementation.

A correctness test confirms that the TP=4 SwiGLU MLP output (after the single all-reduce) matches a single-GPU reference SwiGLU forward pass on identical inputs to within FP16 numerical tolerance across all ranks.

A behavioral check verifies that the TP-partitioned SwiGLU MLP performs the same number of floating-point operations per rank as expected under column-parallel/row-parallel sharding (i.e., no duplicated GEMM work introduced by the partitioning scheme).

The deeply fused SwiGLU operator combining W_Up GEMM, W_Gate GEMM, SiLU, and elementwise multiplication into a single CUDA/Triton kernel — streaming intermediates through Tensor Cores without HBM materialization — is implemented as described in Section 3 and Figure 1(c).
The kernel exposes a well-defined operator interface that replaces the two-kernel SGLang/vLLM SwiGLU path with a single fused launch.

Code has been implemented that defines a DeepFusionKernel operator entry point (Python-callable wrapper) taking input activations X (shape [M, d_model]), W_Up (shape [d_model, d_ff]), and W_Gate (shape [d_model, d_ff]) and returning a single output tensor of shape [M, d_ff] representing SiLU(X @ W_Gate) * (X @ W_Up).

Code has been implemented so that a single invocation of DeepFusionKernel produces the same numerical result (within FP16 tolerance) as the reference PyTorch four-kernel sequence: mul(silu(X @ W_Gate), X @ W_Up).
Code has been implemented that supports FP16 input/weight dtypes (matching the LLaMA 3.1 70B FP16 deployment used in Section 4) and produces an FP16 output tensor.

Code has been implemented so that the fused operator issues exactly ONE kernel launch on the GPU per invocation (verifiable via CUDA profiler / nsys), replacing the 4 launches of the naive PyTorch path (Figure 1(a)) and the 2 launches of the SGLang/vLLM path (Figure 1(b)).
The kernel body fuses the two GEMMs, SiLU, and elementwise multiplication into a single streaming compute pipeline (Figure 1(c) / Section 3).

Code has been implemented that computes both the X @ W_Up and X @ W_Gate matrix products inside the same kernel body (sharing the loaded X tile), rather than dispatching them as separate kernels or subroutines with intermediate HBM writes.

Code has been implemented that applies the SiLU nonlinearity (x * sigmoid(x)) to each Gate GEMM accumulator tile in-register/on-chip immediately after the accumulator is completed, without storing the pre-activation Gate output to HBM.
Code has been implemented that performs the elementwise multiplication of the SiLU(Gate) tile with the corresponding Up-projection tile in-register/on-chip prior to any HBM store of either operand.

Code has been implemented so that the ONLY tensor written to HBM by DeepFusionKernel is the final SiLU(X @ W_Gate) * (X @ W_Up) result — no intermediate Up-projection, Gate-projection, or post-SiLU tensor of full shape [M, d_ff] is materialized in HBM.

Code has been implemented that loads each tile of the input activation X from HBM at most once per output-tile computation and reuses it for both the Up and Gate GEMM inner loops (input-side reuse as motivated in Section 3).
The kernel uses Tensor Cores (MMA / WMMA / Triton tl.dot with tensor-core intrinsics) to execute both GEMMs at high arithmetic intensity.

Code has been implemented that dispatches both the W_Up and W_Gate matrix products through Tensor Core matrix-multiply-accumulate instructions (via Triton tl.dot, CUTLASS MMA, or wmma intrinsics) rather than scalar/CUDA-core FMA loops.
Code has been implemented that keeps GEMM accumulators in FP32 registers during the inner-product loop and casts to FP16 only when writing the final fused output.

Code has been implemented that uses tile shapes compatible with Tensor Core MMA dimensions (e.g., M/N/K multiples of 16 for FP16 on Ampere/Hopper) so that MMA instructions are issued without fallback paths.
The kernel implements shared-memory / register-level tiling for W_Up, W_Gate, and X, and streams the K dimension without spilling intermediates.
Code has been implemented that stages tiles of X, W_Up, and W_Gate into on-chip shared memory (SMEM) before feeding them into Tensor Core MMAs.

Code has been implemented that maintains two concurrent output accumulators (one for the Up projection, one for the Gate projection) within each thread block / warpgroup, so both GEMMs advance together over the shared K loop.

Code has been implemented that iterates over the K (d_model) dimension in a single fused loop that advances both the Up and Gate partial sums per K-tile, rather than running two separate K loops sequentially.
Code has been implemented that exposes BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, and BLOCK_K (or equivalent tile-size) parameters as compile-time / autotune constants of the kernel.

Code has been implemented that uses software pipelining / async copies (cp.async on Ampere, TMA on Hopper, or Triton's num_stages) to overlap HBM loads of the next K-tile with MMA compute on the current tile.
The fused SiLU + elementwise-multiply epilogue is implemented correctly and numerically.
Code has been implemented that computes SiLU as x * sigmoid(x) (equivalently x / (1 + exp(-x))) inside the kernel epilogue, evaluated on the Gate accumulator tile in FP32 before down-casting.

A unit test has been implemented that compares the DeepFusionKernel output against a reference torch implementation (torch.nn.functional.silu(X @ W_Gate) * (X @ W_Up)) on random FP16 inputs of representative LLaMA 3.1 70B MLP shapes and asserts elementwise agreement within FP16 tolerance (e.g., atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2).
The unit test suite covers edge-case shapes with M values (batch*seq) of 1, 4, 16, and 64 — matching batch sizes used in the paper's experiments — and passes for all of them.
The kernel supports the LLaMA 3.1 70B MLP shapes under TP=4 and integrates with the tensor-parallel column-wise sharded W_Up / W_Gate provided by the caller.
Code has been implemented so that the kernel accepts d_model = 8192 and per-rank d_ff shard = 28672/4 = 7168 (LLaMA 3.1 70B, TP=4) as valid input dimensions and executes correctly on those shapes.

Code has been implemented that treats the incoming W_Up and W_Gate tensors as already column-partitioned across TP ranks (per Appendix A.1 / Figure 2) and does NOT insert any additional all-reduce or all-gather inside the fused kernel itself.

Code has been implemented that yields output layout compatible with the downstream row-wise-sharded W_Down GEMM (i.e., output columns correspond to the local d_ff shard on each rank, so the subsequent W_Down + single all-reduce path is preserved).
The kernel is CUDA-Graph-capturable and free of dynamic control flow that would prevent capture inside SGLang's warm-up.

Code has been implemented so that a full DeepFusionKernel invocation on fixed input shapes can be captured inside a torch.cuda.CUDAGraph and replayed to produce identical outputs (bitwise-equal replay).

Code has been implemented such that the kernel launch performs no host-side branching, allocation, or synchronization dependent on tensor values after the initial argument packing (only static grid/block computation from tensor shapes).
Measured HBM-traffic and speedup properties of the standalone fused kernel match the paper's claims (Figure 1(d) / Section 4.2 attribution to fusion).

A microbenchmark has been implemented that, using NVIDIA Nsight Compute (or equivalent), measures HBM bytes read+written per DeepFusionKernel invocation on LLaMA 3.1 70B MLP shapes at M=1 and confirms it is strictly less than the sum of HBM traffic of the SGLang two-kernel baseline on identical inputs.

A microbenchmark has been implemented that measures the wall-clock latency of a single DeepFusionKernel invocation vs. the SGLang two-kernel SwiGLU path on the same LLaMA 3.1 70B MLP shapes on H100, and confirms DeepFusionKernel is faster on at least the small-M regimes (M in {1,4,16}) matching the memory-bound scenarios described in Section 4.4.

Measurement confirms that DeepFusionKernel does NOT increase FLOPs relative to the two-kernel baseline (as asserted in the Figure 1 caption): the total floating-point-operation count per invocation is equal to 2*M*d_model*d_ff (Up) + 2*M*d_model*d_ff (Gate) + O(M*d_ff) elementwise, within a 1% tolerance when profiled.

Row-major and column-major tiling variants of DeepFusionKernel are implemented, with tile sizes tuned to balance register usage, shared-memory occupancy, and Tensor Core utilization, exposing a set of candidate kernels.
The kernel source exposes multiple candidate variants distinguished by loop ordering (row-major vs column-major tiling) so the scheduler can select among them.

Code has been implemented that defines at least two distinct DeepFusionKernel variants (one row-major-tiled, one column-major-tiled) as separately callable kernels or as a single kernel parameterized by a loop-order template/flag.
Code has been implemented that registers all tiling/loop-order variants into a candidate-kernel list or registry that the profiler-driven scheduler can enumerate at deployment time.
Each candidate variant exposes an identifier (name/enum) and a metadata record describing its tiling scheme (row-major vs column-major) and tile-size parameters so results can be logged per variant.
The row-major tiling variant is implemented to maximize reuse of input activation X across the fused W_Up/W_Gate GEMMs.

Code has been implemented in which the row-major variant iterates the outer loop over rows of the input/output tile such that an activation-row tile is loaded once from HBM and reused across the K-dimension GEMM accumulation for both W_Up and W_Gate.

The row-major variant stages activation tiles into shared memory (or registers) before issuing Tensor Core mma instructions, and does not re-load the same activation tile from HBM within a single output-tile computation.

A unit test / correctness check verifies that the row-major variant produces outputs numerically matching (within FP16 tolerance) a reference SwiGLU (W_Up, W_Gate, SiLU, elementwise multiply) computation on random inputs.
The column-major tiling variant is implemented to maximize reuse of weight tiles from W_Up and W_Gate, favoring small-batch / weight-dominated regimes.

Code has been implemented in which the column-major variant iterates the outer loop over output columns (weight-column tiles) so that a loaded W_Up/W_Gate tile is reused across multiple activation rows before being evicted.
The column-major variant stages weight tiles into shared memory once per outer iteration and reuses them for both the W_Up and W_Gate GEMM contributions to the fused output tile.
A unit test / correctness check verifies that the column-major variant produces outputs numerically matching (within FP16 tolerance) a reference SwiGLU computation on random inputs.
Tile sizes (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K or equivalent) are exposed as tunable parameters and multiple tile-size configurations per loop-order variant are enumerated as candidates.

Code has been implemented that parameterizes each kernel variant over tile-size constants (M/N/K block dims) via template arguments, Triton autotune configs, or equivalent, rather than hard-coding a single tile size.
A set of at least three distinct tile-size configurations is registered per loop-order variant, chosen so that the shapes are legal for Tensor Core mma instructions on the target GPU (A100/H100).

The tile-size choices are documented/asserted to keep per-thread register usage and per-block shared-memory usage within the target GPU limits (no launch failures due to resource over-subscription for any registered candidate).
The tiling variants are constructed to exploit Tensor Cores and on-chip resources rather than issuing scalar/CUDA-core-only GEMMs.

Code has been implemented that dispatches the inner GEMM accumulation of each variant through a Tensor Core primitive (wgmma/mma.sync/tl.dot with FP16 inputs) rather than through scalar multiply-add loops.

The kernel variants stream partial GEMM results, SiLU, and elementwise multiplication through registers/shared memory without writing the pre-activation W_Up X or W_Gate X tiles back to HBM as intermediate tensors.

The occupancy characteristics of each registered variant (blocks/SM or threads/SM implied by tile sizes and shared-memory usage) are computable/queryable, e.g., via a helper function or documented derivation, so tuning can trade off occupancy vs reuse.
Behavioral checks confirm that the row-major and column-major variants exhibit their intended reuse trade-offs across workload regimes.

A microbenchmark harness runs each registered candidate variant on representative SwiGLU shapes (LLaMA 3.1 70B TP=4 per-shard MLP dimensions) across at least the batch sizes {1, 4, 16, 64} and records per-variant latency.

The microbenchmark results show that at small batch sizes (weight-dominated regime, e.g., B=1) at least one column-major-tiled variant achieves lower latency than the fastest row-major-tiled variant, consistent with the trade-off claimed in Section 3.

The set of candidate kernels contains at least one variant that, when selected by the scheduler on the H100 TP=4 LLaMA 3.1 70B configuration at B=2, yields a full-model decoding throughput speedup of approximately 13.2% over SGLang, matching the paper's peak H100 gain.

The set of candidate kernels contains at least one variant that, when selected by the scheduler on the A100 TP=4 LLaMA 3.1 70B configuration at B=16, yields a full-model decoding throughput speedup of approximately 9.7% over SGLang, matching the paper's peak A100 gain.

The lightweight profiler-based scheduler that benchmarks candidate fused-kernel variants at deployment time and selects the highest-throughput option per model/workload/hardware is implemented, integrated with CUDA Graph capture to avoid inference-time dispatch overhead.
The scheduler exposes a registry of candidate fused-kernel variants (row-major and column-major tiling of DeepFusionKernel, plus tile-size configurations) that it can enumerate for benchmarking.

Code has been implemented that maintains a data structure (list/dict/registry) enumerating all candidate DeepFusionKernel variants, each identified by tiling scheme (row-major vs column-major) and tile-size parameters.

Code has been implemented that allows candidate kernels to be looked up/filtered by model shape (d_model, d_ff), batch size, and target hardware identifier so the scheduler can restrict the search space per workload.
The profiler benchmarks each candidate kernel on the target hardware at deployment time using representative input shapes and returns a measured timing/throughput per candidate.

Code has been implemented that, given a model configuration and batch size, constructs representative input tensors (matching the SwiGLU MLP's actual shapes under TP=4) and invokes each candidate kernel for timing.

Code has been implemented that performs warm-up iterations before timing and uses CUDA event-based (or equivalently accurate GPU-synchronized) measurement to avoid host-side timing noise when benchmarking each candidate.
Code has been implemented that runs multiple measurement iterations per candidate and aggregates (mean or median) the per-candidate timing to reduce measurement variance.

The end-to-end profiling step for the DeepFusionKernel candidate set completes as a short pre-inference phase (bounded overhead, one-shot per deployment) rather than running repeatedly during inference.
The scheduler selects the highest-throughput candidate from the profiling results and adapts the choice to model shape, batch size, and GPU microarchitecture.

Code has been implemented that, given the per-candidate benchmark results, picks the variant with the best measured throughput and records it as the active kernel for the (model, batch size, hardware) key.

The scheduler produces different selections consistent with the paper's observations: for small batch sizes / weight-dominated regimes it can select the column-major (weight-tile-reusing) variant, and for larger batch / activation-dominated regimes it can select the row-major variant.
The scheduler's selection is re-run (or re-keyed) when moving between A100 and H100 clusters so that the chosen kernel variant reflects the target GPU microarchitecture rather than being hard-coded.
The scheduler is integrated with SGLang's CUDA Graph capture so that once the best kernel is selected, it is baked into the captured graph and no scheduling/dispatch logic runs during inference.
Code has been implemented that fixes the selected kernel variant before SGLang's CUDA Graph warm-up/capture phase so that the graph records calls to only the chosen kernel implementation.

The inference-time forward path contains no Python-level branching or scheduler dispatch across candidate kernels (the graph replay directly executes the pre-selected kernel), verifiable by inspection of the captured graph / execution trace.
The scheduler-plus-CUDA-Graph pipeline runs end-to-end within SGLang with the FlashInfer attention backend enabled and successfully serves LLaMA 3.1 70B decoding without falling back to eager mode.
The scheduler yields the paper's measured behavior: robust speedups across regimes with no recurring inference-time dispatch overhead.

With the profiler-driven scheduler active, the DeepFusionKernel-in-SGLang pipeline achieves a peak speedup of approximately 9.7% over default SGLang on A100 for LLaMA 3.1 70B FP16 TP=4 decoding (input length 1, output length 1024) at the batch size where SwiGLU is most memory-bound.

With the profiler-driven scheduler active, the pipeline achieves a peak speedup of approximately 13.2% over default SGLang on H100 for LLaMA 3.1 70B FP16 TP=4 decoding (input length 1, output length 1024).

The per-inference-step runtime measured with the scheduler active is indistinguishable (within measurement noise) from running the pre-selected kernel directly under the same CUDA Graph, confirming zero recurring dispatch overhead.
DeepFusionKernel and its scheduler are integrated inside SGLang with the FlashInfer attention backend and CUDA Graphs enabled, reusing SGLang's existing all-reduce and collective primitives.
SGLang is configured with the FlashInfer attention backend and CUDA Graph capture enabled as the runtime host for DeepFusionKernel.

Code has been implemented that launches SGLang for LLaMA 3.1 70B decoding with `--attention-backend flashinfer` (or equivalent programmatic setting) so that FlashInfer serves attention for all DeepFusionKernel experiments.

Code has been implemented that enables CUDA Graph capture in SGLang (i.e., CUDA Graphs are not disabled via `--disable-cuda-graph`) so that captured graphs include the DeepFusionKernel call for the selected variant.
Code has been implemented that launches the SGLang server/engine with tensor-parallel size 4 (`--tp 4`) using LLaMA 3.1 70B in FP16 on a single node of 4 GPUs.
DeepFusionKernel is registered inside SGLang as a drop-in replacement for the default fused SwiGLU MLP path, so that model forward calls dispatch to the fused operator.

Code has been implemented that patches or subclasses SGLang's LLaMA MLP module so that the SwiGLU (W_Up GEMM + W_Gate GEMM + SiLU + elementwise multiply) forward path invokes DeepFusionKernel instead of SGLang's default two-kernel implementation.

The registered DeepFusionKernel entry point accepts the same input tensors (hidden states, column-parallel W_Up and W_Gate shards) and returns a tensor with the same shape/dtype as SGLang's default fused SwiGLU path, so downstream layers (W_Down, all-reduce) are unchanged.

Code has been implemented so that the DeepFusionKernel call is captureable by CUDA Graphs (no dynamic shape branching, no host-side control flow, no per-call allocations) once the scheduler has selected a variant.
DeepFusionKernel reuses SGLang's existing all-reduce and collective primitives without modifying communication patterns.

The integrated MLP path issues exactly one all-reduce per SwiGLU block (after W_Down), matching SGLang's TP collective schedule, and DeepFusionKernel does not introduce any additional all-reduce, all-gather, or reduce-scatter calls.

Code has been implemented so that the SGLang custom cross-device all-reduce kernel (SGLang's default TP collective) is used unchanged around the fused MLP; DeepFusionKernel does not fall back to torch.distributed all-reduce.
The profiler-driven kernel scheduler is wired into SGLang's startup path so that variant selection happens once before CUDA Graph capture.

Code has been implemented that runs the DeepFusionKernel scheduler during SGLang's warm-up phase (before CUDA Graph capture) to benchmark candidate kernel variants on the target hardware and record the chosen variant.

After scheduler selection, the chosen DeepFusionKernel variant (tiling / loop order / tile sizes) is bound into the module before CUDA Graph capture, so that inference-time dispatch has no per-token branching or scheduler overhead.

Code has been implemented so that the scheduler is re-invoked (or its cache is keyed) per (GPU type, TP size, model shape, batch size) configuration, ensuring the best variant is selected for each of the A100 and H100 clusters and each batch size evaluated.
The SGLang+DeepFusionKernel integration produces functionally correct decoding outputs equivalent to default SGLang.

A correctness test has been implemented that decodes the same prompt with default SGLang and SGLang+DeepFusionKernel under identical seeds/settings and verifies that generated token IDs match (or logits agree within FP16 numerical tolerance).

A behavioral check has been implemented (e.g., via NSight or CUDA Graph replay counters) confirming that after warm-up, the scheduler's profiling code is not executed during measured decoding steps, so per-iteration dispatch overhead from the scheduler is zero.

Naive distributed PyTorch, default SGLang, and vLLM baseline decoding pipelines for LLaMA 3.1 70B under TP=4 are set up correctly and produce comparable measurements to the paper's reported baseline numbers.

Common baseline decoding harness configures LLaMA 3.1 70B in FP16 with TP=4 across four GPUs, fixed input length 1, output length 1024 by default, batch sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, four repetitions per configuration, and reports mean throughput (tokens/s) and standard deviation of the decoding stage only.
Code has been implemented that loads LLaMA 3.1 70B weights and enforces FP16 precision (torch.float16 / half-precision execution) for all three baseline pipelines (PyTorch, SGLang, vLLM).
Code has been implemented that launches all three baselines with tensor-parallel size TP=4 across four GPUs on a single node.
The baseline benchmark driver sets prompt/input length to 1 and target output length to 1024 tokens for the full-model throughput experiment.
Code has been implemented that sweeps batch sizes over {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} for the full-model throughput measurement.
Each (framework, batch size, GPU) configuration is measured four times and the driver computes and records both mean and standard deviation of decoding throughput.
The measurement harness excludes prefill/warm-up and reports only decoding-stage throughput (tokens/s) so results are comparable across PyTorch, SGLang, and vLLM.

Analytical conclusions from Section 4.4 are reproduced: DeepFusionKernel yields the largest gains in memory-bandwidth-bound regimes (small batches, large models, long contexts), maintains benefit on H100 across a wider batch range with diminishing returns at very large batches, throughput variance grows with batch size due to inter-GPU jitter, and MLP remains a significant per-token latency fraction even for long sequences.

Code has been implemented to compute DeepFusionKernel speedup over SGLang (and over vLLM) as (throughput_DFK / throughput_baseline - 1) for every (GPU, batch size, output length) cell.
Code has been implemented to compute the coefficient of variation (std/mean) of throughput for each (framework, GPU, batch size, output length) configuration to enable variance-vs-batch analysis.
Memory-bandwidth-bound regime claims: fusion gains are largest at small batch sizes on A100, and remain significant on H100 across a wider batch-size range.
On A100 at TP=4, LLaMA 3.1 70B FP16, input length 1 and output length 1024, DeepFusionKernel achieves its peak speedup over SGLang at batch size 16, reaching approximately +9.7%.
On H100 at TP=4, LLaMA 3.1 70B FP16, input length 1 and output length 1024, DeepFusionKernel achieves its peak speedup over SGLang at batch size 2, reaching approximately +13.2%.

Code has been implemented to test the claim that on A100 the DeepFusionKernel-vs-SGLang speedup peaks in the small-to-moderate batch regime (batches 1-16) and declines toward the largest batch (64), consistent with A100 being more strongly memory-bandwidth-bound at small batches.
On H100, DeepFusionKernel achieves a positive speedup over SGLang across all evaluated batch sizes 1 through 64 in the Table 1 sweep, demonstrating benefit across a wider batch-size range than A100.
On H100 the DeepFusionKernel-vs-SGLang speedup at the largest batch (B=64) is smaller than the H100 peak speedup, demonstrating diminishing marginal returns at very large batches.

Throughput-variance claim: measured standard deviation of throughput grows with batch size across frameworks, attributable to inter-GPU communication jitter that DeepFusionKernel inherits from SGLang's unchanged collective primitives.

Code has been implemented to verify that in the Table 1 measurements, the throughput standard deviation for SGLang and DeepFusionKernel on both A100 and H100 exhibits an overall increasing trend with batch size from B=1 to B=64.

The throughput standard deviation for the naive Torch distributed baseline at large batch sizes (B=32, B=64) on both A100 and H100 is substantially larger (order of magnitude) than at B=1, consistent with communication jitter dominating variance at high batch sizes.

The measurement protocol for regime analysis reuses SGLang's default all-reduce/collective primitives when running the DeepFusionKernel variant (no replacement communication kernels), so any observed variance is attributable to the shared collective path rather than to fusion-specific communication changes.

Long-context / MLP-latency claim: even as output length grows and KV-cache/attention costs increase, the SwiGLU MLP remains a significant fraction of per-token latency, so DeepFusionKernel produces persistent gains across long-generation lengths.

In the Table 2 long-generation sweep (output lengths 1024, 4096, 16384; batch sizes 1, 4, 16; A100 and H100), DeepFusionKernel achieves the highest throughput of the three frameworks (SGLang, vLLM, DeepFusionKernel) in every reported (GPU, batch size, output length) cell.

For each (GPU, batch size) pair in Table 2, the DeepFusionKernel-vs-SGLang throughput speedup remains strictly positive as output length increases from 1024 to 16384, demonstrating that MLP fusion continues to yield gains at long generation lengths.

Code has been implemented to compute the relative throughput drop (throughput at 16384 vs 1024 output length) for each framework and to report that the drop is comparable in magnitude across SGLang, vLLM, and DeepFusionKernel, supporting the claim that DeepFusionKernel does not lose its MLP-side advantage as attention/KV costs grow.
Consolidated regime-analysis reporting reproduces the qualitative conclusions of Section 4.4.
